body:
## Problem

`power-guard` never notices when its `systemd-inhibit` child dies. The daemon's only protection against UPower's single-sample CriticalPowerAction is the block inhibitor it holds while it confirms a critical reading (#1687); if that child exits, the guard keeps believing it holds the block for the rest of the process lifetime, logs nothing, and never tries to re-engage — so the machine is exactly as unguarded as if power-guard were not running, while the daemon reports a healthy state.

## Evidence

`nixos/services/power-guard/power-guard.py` @ `2bcd46e0dc`:

- `Inhibitor.engage()` (:153-173): returns immediately when `self.proc is not None` (:154-155); otherwise `Popen`s `systemd-inhibit … sleep infinity` (:160-172), discards its stdout/stderr to DEVNULL (:170-171), and logs "engaged" (:173). Nothing ever calls `poll()` / `wait()` on the child.
- `Inhibitor.held` (:183-185): `return self.proc is not None` — handle non-None is treated as lock held, regardless of whether the process is alive.
- `Inhibitor.release()` (:175-181) is the only place `self.proc` returns to `None` (plus `terminate()` without `wait()`).
- Main loop (:208-215): the low-battery path calls `inh.engage()` every poll; with a dead child every one of those calls is a no-op.

Verified this run on the laptop (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-pg-inhibit`, real `power-guard.py`, stub `systemd-inhibit` on PATH):

- Stub exits 1 immediately: after `engage()`, `inh.proc.poll() == 1` (child dead) yet `inh.held == True`; a second `engage()` did not invoke `systemd-inhibit` again (stub invocation log: exactly 1 call). The daemon would sit in this state forever.
- Control (stub `exec sleep 30`): `poll() is None`, `held == True`, `release()` clears `held` — the live path works as intended.

A child can die for ordinary reasons: `systemd-inhibit` failing to acquire the lock, the inhibitor being killed, a logind restart/reload, or the `sleep infinity` being signalled. Because stderr goes to DEVNULL, even the child's own complaint is invisible.

## Why it matters

The guard exists because of the 2026-10-28 incident (#1687): UPower hybrid-slept the laptop for 2h40m on a glitched reading. A silently dead inhibitor recreates that exact exposure with a false sense of coverage — the unit is active, the log says "INHIBIT(block sleep) engaged", and the first glitched critical sample sleeps the machine. Silent loss of a safety control is worse than the control failing loudly.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The daemon detects a dead inhibitor child (e.g. `held` reflects `poll() is None` for a real process, checked on engage and/or each poll cycle).
- [ ] On detection it acts, per a stated policy: re-engage the inhibitor (logging the death and the child's exit status loudly) and/or exit non-zero so the unit surfaces as failed — it must not continue indefinitely believing it holds a lock it does not hold.
- [ ] The child's stderr is no longer unconditionally discarded, or its exit status is logged on death, so the failure is diagnosable from the journal.
- [ ] `release()` reaps the child (`wait()` or equivalent) instead of leaving a zombie.
- [ ] Tests in `test_power_guard.py` (the suite added for #6477) cover: a child that exits immediately is detected and handled; a live child is not disturbed; the NO_INHIBIT stub path is unchanged.
- [ ] Existing power-guard tests still pass.
